name: Gujarati

script.overview:
Gujarati is written in its own script, an **abugida** read left to right. Each consonant letter carries an inherent vowel *a* (ક = *ka*); other vowels are added as **vowel signs** (કા *kā*, કિ *ki*, કુ *ku*, કે *ke*). Independent vowel letters (અ, આ, ઇ…) are used only at the start of a word or after another vowel.

The biggest visual difference from Devanagari is that **Gujarati has no headline (shirorekha)**: Hindi घर hangs from a top bar, Gujarati ઘર does not. Many letters are simply Devanagari shapes without the bar (ગ, ન, મ), while others differ noticeably (ક, ખ, જ, ફ, શ, લ, ળ). Gujarati also has a letter Hindi lacks: **ળ** (retroflex ḷ).

To write a consonant with no vowel, add the **virama** (્): ક્. In practice consonants with no vowel between them are fused into **conjuncts**: સ્ત (st), ત્ર (tr), ક્ષ (kṣ). ર is written as a small hook on top (reph) when it comes first in a cluster (ધર્મ *dharm*) and as a small stroke underneath when it comes second (પ્ર *pr*).

The inherent *a* is often silent at the end of words and in the middle of many words (schwa deletion), exactly as in Hindi. Gujarati has its own **digits** (૧ ૨ ૩ …), though Western digits are also very common today. Full stop is a normal period (.), not the Hindi danda.

where: Gujarat (India), Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Mumbai; diaspora in the UK, East Africa, North America and the Gulf
tagline: The warm, quick-witted language of Gujarat's traders, poets and kitchens — and of Gandhi — spoken from Ahmedabad to Leicester to Nairobi.
intro:
**Gujarati** (ગુજરાતી, *gujarātī*) is an Indo-Aryan language, a close cousin of Hindi, Rajasthani and Marathi. It is the official language of Gujarat and the mother tongue of Mahatma Gandhi, and thanks to centuries of trade it is heard in markets and family kitchens from Mumbai to Mombasa to London.

Gujarati has its own script, which grew out of the same Nagari tradition as Hindi's Devanagari but dropped the horizontal headline. If you know Devanagari you will recognise many letters immediately; if you don't, the script is regular and quick to learn.

Grammatically, Gujarati is a verb-final (subject–object–verb) language with **three genders** (masculine, feminine and neuter — unlike Hindi), **postpositions that attach to nouns as suffixes** (ઘરમાં *gharmāṃ* 'in the house', રામનું *rāmnuṃ* 'Ram's'), and an **ergative past tense** where the doer takes -e (મેં ચા પીધી *meṃ chā pīdhī* 'I drank tea').

This course teaches the **standard modern spoken Gujarati of Ahmedabad and Vadodara**, with notes on common colloquial and regional forms (Kathiawadi, Surati). You'll learn to choose between the intimate **તું** *tuṃ*, the everyday polite **તમે** *tame*, and the very respectful **આપ** *āp*.
romanizationNote: Long vowels are written ā ī ū. Gujarati spelling distinguishes i/ī and u/ū, but in everyday speech they sound the same length — so don't strain over them. **ṃ** marks a nasal vowel: the very common neuter ending -ું is a nasalised u (*sāruṃ*, *māruṃ*), never 'um'. After a long vowel the anusvara is always a nasal vowel ṃ (*pāṃch*, *sāṃj*, *lāṃbuṃ*, *īṃḍuṃ*); after a short vowel before a consonant it is written as the matching nasal consonant (*pandar*, *ṭhaṇḍī*, *raṅg*). The letters e and o can be close (as in *say*, *go*) or open (ɛ as in *bed*, ɔ as in British *hot*); spelling doesn't show this, and an h written between vowels (*bahen*, *kahe*, *mahel*) is usually not a full h but a breathy 'murmur' on the open vowel — see Pronunciation. The silent inherent a is dropped as in speech (છોકરો *chhokro*, not *chhokaro*). **ch** is unaspirated, **chh** aspirated; a doubled aspirate is written with the aspiration once, as it is pronounced (છઠ્ઠું *chhaṭṭhuṃ*, ચોખ્ખું *chokkhuṃ*); **ṭ ḍ ṇ ḷ** are retroflex; ફ is written **f** because that is how most Gujaratis say it; ષ is written **ṣ** but pronounced like sh; ઋ is pronounced and written **ru**; જ્ઞ is **gn**.

pronunciation.title: Aspirated vs unaspirated consonants
pronunciation.body:
Gujarati distinguishes plain consonants (ક ચ ટ ત પ) from aspirated ones (ખ છ ઠ થ ફ) which are released with a clear puff of air. English speakers add a puff automatically at the start of words ('pin', 'top') and none after s ('spin', 'stop') — in Gujarati the puff changes the meaning, so you must control it.

The voiced series has the same contrast: બ vs ભ, દ vs ધ, ગ vs ઘ, જ vs ઝ. The 'aspirated' voiced sounds are really **breathy** (murmured): the voice is on but the vocal folds are slack and let air through, like a sigh. In fast Gujarati speech the breathiness often moves onto the following vowel rather than sounding like a separate h.
tips: Hold a strip of paper in front of your lips: it should stay still for ક પ ત and flutter for ખ ફ થ.
To get unaspirated ક, think of the k in 'skin', then drop the s.
For ભ ધ ઘ, say the consonant with a slightly sighing, breathy vowel after it — don't insert a full English h.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex vs dental: ટ ડ vs ત દ
pronunciation.body:
English t and d are made on the gum ridge, in between Gujarati's two series. **Dental** ત થ દ ધ ન touch the back of the upper teeth (a soft, 'French' t). **Retroflex** ટ ઠ ડ ઢ ણ are made with the tongue tip curled back to the roof of the mouth, giving a hollow, hard sound.

If you use your English t for both, Gujaratis will usually hear it as retroflex — so practise the dental ones especially. Many common words differ only in this: વાત 'talk' vs વાટ 'wick; waiting', સાથ 'company' vs સાઠ 'sixty'.
tips: For ત દ, put your tongue tip right against your top teeth — it may even peek out slightly.
For ટ ડ, curl the tip back until the underside touches the roof of your mouth, then flick it forward.
Retroflex sounds colour the vowel next to them; listen for the slight 'r'-like tinge.

pronunciation.title: The retroflex lateral ળ
pronunciation.body:
Gujarati has two l-sounds. લ is an ordinary clear l. **ળ** is made like a retroflex consonant: curl the tongue tip back to the roof of the mouth and let the air flow around the sides. It never starts a word, but it is extremely common: કેળું 'banana', પીળું 'yellow', દાળ 'lentils', ગોળ 'jaggery; round' and every form of મળવું 'to meet'.

Hindi speakers replace ળ with ल, so you will hear Gujaratis from Mumbai or the diaspora do the same — but in Gujarat ળ is alive and it distinguishes words.
tips: Start from ડ: hold the tongue in the ḍ position and say l instead.
Practise ખોલો (open!) vs ખોળો (lap) until a Gujarati can tell which one you mean.
Don't over-curl: the flap is quick and light between vowels.

pronunciation.title: Close e/o vs open ɛ/ɔ
pronunciation.body:
Gujarati has two e-sounds and two o-sounds, but the script writes each with one letter. Close **e** and **o** are pure vowels like the ay in 'say' and the o in 'go' without the English glide. Open **ɛ** and **ɔ** are like the e in 'bed' and the o in British 'hot' (or the aw in 'law').

The open vowels appear above all where the spelling has a + h + e/o: બહેન 'sister' is said [bɛ̤n], મહેલ 'palace' [mɛ̤l], શહેર 'city' [ʃɛ̤ɾ], પહેલું 'first' [pɛ̤lũ], મહોર 'seal' [mɔ̤ɾ]. The h disappears and leaves the vowel open and breathy. They also occur in English loanwords, which careful writers mark with ઍ and ઑ (ઑફિસ 'office', ડૉક્ટર 'doctor').

This course writes both as plain e/o in romanization; listen to the audio and learn the open vowel with the word.
tips: Whenever you see -ahe- or -aho- in spelling, expect a single open, slightly breathy vowel: bahen → 'bɛn'.
Keep close e/o pure — don't let them slide to 'ey'/'ow' as in English.
Words with ઑ/ૉ always have open ɔ.

pronunciation.title: Breathy (murmured) vowels
pronunciation.body:
One of the most characteristic sounds of Gujarati is **breathy voice** (murmur): a vowel spoken with a relaxed, slightly sighing voice. It comes from two sources.

1. **A written h between or after vowels** usually is not pronounced as a separate h. Instead it makes the neighbouring vowel breathy: બહાર 'outside' sounds like [bä̤ɾ], close to બાર 'twelve' but with a murmured ā. ચાહ 'affection' vs ચા 'tea' work the same way.

2. **Voiced aspirates** ભ ધ ઘ ઝ ઢ often lose their puff and pass the breathiness to the following vowel: ભાત 'rice' is roughly [bä̤t̪].

Murmur is subtle but meaningful, and getting it right is a big step towards sounding Gujarati rather than Hindi.
tips: Practise by sighing: say 'aah' as if relieved — that slack voice is murmur.
Don't pronounce a strong English h in બહાર, નહાવું, મહેમાન; let the vowel carry it.
Murmured vowels often sound slightly lower in pitch; copy the melody.

pronunciation.title: The silent inherent a (schwa deletion)
pronunciation.body:
Every consonant letter carries an inherent a, but in speech it is very often dropped. As in Hindi, the a is silent **at the end of a word** (ઘર = *ghar*, not *ghara*) and usually **in the middle of a word when a vowel follows the next consonant**: છોકરો is *chhokro*, દીકરી *dīkrī*, સમજવું *samajvuṃ*.

The practical rule: in a sequence V-C-a-C-V, the a goes silent. Compounds keep each part's pronunciation (બહેન+પણી = *bahenpaṇī*). Sanskrit words often keep a final a after a cluster (શૂન્ય *shūnya*, કૃષ્ણ *kruṣṇa*).

Our romanization already drops the silent a, so follow the roman when in doubt.
tips: Never add a final a after a single consonant: ઘર ghar, રાત rāt, દૂધ dūdh.
Verb infinitives: કરવું karvuṃ, સમજવું samajvuṃ — the a before -vuṃ disappears.
If a word sounds too long and 'spelled out', you're probably pronouncing a silent a.

pronunciation.title: Nasal vowels and the anusvara
pronunciation.body:
The dot above the line (ં, anusvara) does two jobs. Before a consonant in many Sanskrit-derived words it is a real nasal consonant matching the next sound: પંદર *pandar*, સુંદર *sundar*, રંગ *raṅg*. Elsewhere — and especially at the end of a word — it **nasalises the vowel**: air goes through the nose while you say the vowel, with no n or m closure. હું 'I', છું 'am', માં 'in', and the neuter ending -ું (*sāruṃ*, *māruṃ*) are all nasal vowels.

Nasalisation is grammatical in Gujarati: it marks the neuter plural (છોકરાં 'children' vs છોકરા 'boys') and distinguishes મા 'mother' from માં 'in'.
tips: Say 'uh-huh' with your mouth closed, then open it: that nasal resonance is what ં adds.
For final -uṃ, round your lips for u and don't close them: it is not 'um'.
Pinch your nose: a nasal vowel should sound blocked, an oral one should not change.

pronunciation.title: s, sh and the affricates ch / chh
pronunciation.body:
Standard Gujarati has **s** (સ) and **sh** (શ and ષ, which sound identical). Keep them apart: સાલ 'year' vs શાલ 'shawl'.

The palatals ચ છ જ ઝ are affricates, like English ch and j. ચ has no puff; છ has a strong one. છ is everywhere because it starts the verb 'to be': છે, છું, છો.

**Regional note:** in Kathiawadi (Saurashtra) and Surati speech, છ is often said as s (*se* for છે), and s may become h (*hāruṃ* for સારું). You will hear this constantly in films and comedy; understand it, but use the standard sounds yourself.
tips: છે should sound like a breathy 'chhay', not 'chay' and not 'she'.
ષ is just sh — ભાષા bhāṣā sounds like 'bhāshā'.
If someone says 'kem so?' they are asking 'kem chho?' in Kathiawadi style.

pronunciation.title: f, z and English loanwords
pronunciation.body:
Gujarati has absorbed thousands of English, Persian and Arabic words, but its script has no nukta in everyday use. Instead:

- **ફ** is pronounced **f** by most speakers in all words, native or borrowed (ફૂલ *fūl* 'flower', ફોન *fon*). An aspirated p is heard in careful or rural speech.
- **ઝ** stands for English **z** in loans (ઝીરો 'zero'), and જ is used for Persian z (જમીન *jamīn* 'land', from zamīn).
- English short a and o are written with **ઍ** and **ઑ** (ઍક્ટર, ઑફિસ), though many people write plain એ/ઓ.
- English t and d become **retroflex** ટ ડ (ટેબલ, ડૉક્ટર), and English th becomes dental થ (થૅન્ક યુ).
tips: Say ફ as a relaxed f; nobody will misunderstand you.
Pronounce English loans the Gujarati way (retroflex ṭ/ḍ, tapped r) — it sounds more natural in a Gujarati sentence.
Persian-origin words in Gujarati use j for z: જરૂર jarūr 'need', બજાર bajār 'market'.

pronunciation.title: ડ and ઢ between vowels: the flap
pronunciation.body:
At the start of a word or after a nasal, ડ and ઢ are retroflex stops (ડાબું, ઠંડું). **Between vowels and at the end of a word** they are pronounced as quick retroflex **flaps** [ɽ ɽʱ]: the tongue tip curls back and flicks forward across the roof of the mouth, briefly striking it. Hindi writes this with a dot (ड़); Gujarati doesn't mark it at all.

So ઘોડો 'horse' is *gho-ṛo*, લાડુ 'laddoo' *lā-ṛu*, ઝાડ 'tree' *jhāṛ*. We keep ḍ in the romanization, but say a flap.
tips: Start with American 'butter' (a flap), then curl the tongue back — that's the Gujarati flap.
Don't stop the air completely between vowels; the flap is very brief.
ઢ between vowels is the same flap plus breathy voice: દાઢી dāḍhī 'beard'.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants and clusters
pronunciation.body:
A doubled consonant (written with a conjunct like ત્ત, ક્ક, ઠ્ઠ) is held for about twice as long: સત્તર *sat-tar* 'seventeen'. Shortening it can make you sound unclear or produce a different word. English has this only across word boundaries ('book case', 'cat tail').

Two clusters have special Gujarati pronunciations: **ક્ષ** is *ksh* (પરીક્ષા *parīkṣā*), and **જ્ઞ** is *gn* (જ્ઞાન *gnān* 'knowledge') — different from Hindi's 'gy'. Clusters with r (પ્ર, ત્ર, ક્ર) are said with a light tap, never an English r.
tips: Pause very slightly on the doubled consonant: chok-kas, gus-so.
Don't insert a vowel inside clusters: ત્રણ is traṇ, not taraṇ.
જ્ઞ = gn: say 'gnān' as one syllable start, as in 'ignore' without the i.

pronunciation.title: Question intonation and little particles
pronunciation.body:
A statement becomes a yes/no question just by **rising intonation** at the end: તમે ગુજરાતી છો. 'You are Gujarati.' → તમે ગુજરાતી છો? 'Are you Gujarati?' In more careful speech, શું can be put at the start (શું તમે ગુજરાતી છો?).

Questions with question words (ક્યાં, શું, કેમ) usually fall at the end. Gujarati conversation is full of small particles that carry tone: **ને** (tag 'right?' or a softener in requests: આવો ને! 'do come!'), **જ** (emphasis, 'only, exactly'), **તો** ('so, well'), **હેં?** ('huh?'). Getting their melody right makes you sound natural.
tips: Practise the same sentence as a statement and a question; only the last syllable's pitch changes.
Use ને with a gentle rise to soften requests: બેસો ને.
Stress in Gujarati is light and fairly even — don't hammer one syllable as in English.
